claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among the ternary, quaternary, and quinary Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloys are governed primarily by composition-dependent local stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes an earlier onset of mechanical twinning or transformation-induced plasticity.
Mechanical twinning or transformation-induced plasticity increases strain-hardening capacity.
Mechanical twinning or transformation-induced plasticity increases ultimate strength.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors cross-slip-dominated deformation.
Higher stacking-fault energy produces lower work-hardening rates.
Changing or partially substituting Mn, Fe, or Co can produce controlled differences in stacking-fault energy among Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni subsets.
Stacking-fault energy controls the balance among dislocation slip, mechanical twinning, and strain-induced martensitic transformation in FCC Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni-derived alloys.
Lower stacking-fault energy increases partial-dislocation activity.
Lower stacking-fault energy increases the propensity for deformation twins or martensite.
Twin or martensite formation raises strain hardening and delays necking.
Higher-stacking-fault-energy compositions deform predominantly by perfect-dislocation slip.
Alloys below the quinary CrMnFeCoNi baseline stacking-fault energy will exhibit earlier twinning or TRIP, greater strain hardening, and higher ultimate strength.
Alloys above the quinary baseline stacking-fault-energy range will exhibit reduced strain hardening but enhanced ductility under otherwise identical conditions.
Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can serve as a single-phase FCC baseline.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys that remain single-phase FCC and lack significant precipitation.
High temperatures or prolonged thermal exposure can promote intermetallic formation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Substantial differences in processing history can invalidate the proposed stacking-fault-energy-controlled relationship.
Local chemical fluctuations and metastable phase formation can complicate prediction of strength–ductility trade-offs from nominal composition and stacking-fault energy.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that lower-SFE twinning or martensite formation delays necking, which ordinarily implies improved uniform ductility, while the predicted outcome instead assigns enhanced ductility to the higher-SFE alloys. The intended ductility trend is therefore internally ambiguous.
